sentences.text: The name Deinosuchus comes from the Greek words deinos, meaning terrible, and suchos, meaning crocodile.
This extinct genus belongs to the order Crocodilia and the superfamily Alligatoroidea, and it was substantially larger than any living crocodilian today.
It possessed a broad, alligator-like snout with a slightly bulbous tip and large, robust teeth adapted for crushing.
The largest known individuals surpassed 9 meters in total length, though the maximum estimated size is between 9 and 10 meters.
Estimates for the bite force of Deinosuchus range from 18,000 N to 102,803 N.
Based on growth rings in dorsal osteoderms, estimates indicate it may have taken Deinosuchus nearly 35 years to reach full adult size, with some individuals living over 50 years.
The genus Deinosuchus was first described by Holland in 1909, and the genus was established by Holland in 1909.
A large tooth likely belonging to Deinosuchus was named Polydectes biturgidus by Edward Drinker Cope in 1869.
Fossils of this large alligatoroid have been found in ten US states and northern Mexico.

Deinosuchus was likely capable of killing and eating large dinosaurs, a hypothesis supported by Colbert and Bird in 1954 who speculated it hunted and devoured dinosaurs, and Colbert in 1961 who stated it hunted dinosaurs in the water where giant theropods could not reach.
Schwimmer in 2002 noted hadrosaurid vertebrae with Deinosuchus tooth marks, supporting the idea it fed on dinosaurs, while Brochu in 2003 agreed that Deinosuchus likely ate ornithopods occasionally.
A 2014 study suggested Deinosuchus could perform a death roll similar to modern crocodiles.
The osteoderms and connective tissue of Deinosuchus acted as load-bearing reinforcement to support its massive body on land.
A 1999 study by Gregory M. Erickson and Christopher A. Brochu suggested that Deinosuchus had a growth rate comparable to modern crocodilians but maintained over a longer period.
Schwimmer noted that no theropod dinosaurs of comparable size are known from the eastern range of Deinosuchus, indicating it may have been the apex predator of the region.
Deinosuchus is an extinct genus of diapsid saurians belonging to the order Crocodilia and the superfamily Alligatoroidea.
A 2025 study by Walter and colleagues argues that many traits thought diagnostic for alligatoroids are actually more widespread.

Deinosuchus lived during the Late Cretaceous, approximately 82 million years ago, and the oldest Deinosuchus lived approximately 82 million years ago, while the youngest lived around 73 million years ago.

Deinosuchus lived in North America, including present-day United States and northern Mexico, approximately 80 to 75 million years ago, and in the Aguja Formation of Texas, where some of the largest Deinosuchus specimens were found, these predators likely inhabited brackish-water bays.

Walter and colleagues in 2025 argued previous size estimates were too high due to incorrect scaling, estimating maximum lengths of 10.5 m for D. riograndensis and 7.64 m for D. schwimmeri, and suggested that Purussaurus was likely larger than Deinosuchus. In 2002, Schwimmer debated whether Deinosuchus growth rings reflected annual periods, suggesting they could have been affected by migrations, climate, or ocean cycles. Colbert and Bird miscalculated the skull proportions, causing the reconstruction to greatly exaggerate both its length and width. While often described as the largest crocodilian of all time, some other crocodiliforms including Purussaurus, Rhamphosuchus, and Sarcosuchus may have equaled or exceeded its size.
